description: An overview of Georgia law on the liability of owners and keepers of vicious dogs, from the "first bite rule" to the 1985 leash law amendment.
shortAnswer: Georgia dog bite law has grown more favorable to injury victims over the last few decades. Because of the 1985 amendment, if your child has been bitten by a dog and you suspect the owner/keeper of that dog was violating a "leash law" or local restrictive ordinance, you may have a great chance of getting compensation for your child's injury.

faq.q: What is Georgia's "first bite rule" for dog attacks?
faq.a: Under that rule an owner or keeper of a vicious dog could be held liable for their dog's behavior only if the animal had previously exhibited a propensity to bite or attack and the owner/keeper knew of the dog's vicious propensity. It was understood by many as giving dog owners "one free bite."

faq.q: Is a Georgia dog owner liable if their dog was off its leash when it bit my child?
faq.a: If you can prove that the dog's owner or keeper committed a violation of an applicable "leash law," then the "one bite rule" does not apply. No proof of knowledge about the dog's previous vicious propensity is needed. Appellate cases have applied this to restrictive ordinances that require an owner to keep a dog confined to the property, too.

faq.q: Is a dog owner responsible if my child provoked the dog?
faq.a: If the bite or attack was provoked by teasing or other actions that incited the dog, the owner or keeper cannot be held accountable for their animal's actions. According to historic Georgia law, dog owners are not responsible for provoked actions of an otherwise friendly animal.

faq.q: What if there is no leash law where my child was bitten?
faq.a: Some parks have rules that require owners/keepers to keep dogs on a leash. Also, under "negligent undertaking," if the dog owner/keeper voluntarily agrees to restrain their dog but then fails to do so properly, resulting in an injury, the owner can be held responsible.
